We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Biases Propagate in Encoder-based Vision-Language Models: A Systematic Analysis From Intrinsic Measures to Zero-shot Retrieval Outcomes
papers.research_question: How do social-group biases intrinsic to foundational encoder-based vision-language models (VLMs) manifest in biases in downstream zero-shot retrieval tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a controlled framework to measure the propagation of social-group biases from intrinsic model representations to extrinsic zero-shot retrieval outcomes, demonstrating strong correlations and that larger models exhibit greater bias propagation.
papers.conclusion: Biases in encoder-based VLMs propagate with high and systematically varying correlations to zero-shot retrieval outcomes, with larger models showing greater propagation, leading to detrimental performance implications for marginalized groups.
papers.key_findings:
Strong positive correlations (average Spearman's ρ = 0.83 ± 0.10) exist between intrinsic biases in VLM representations and extrinsic biases in zero-shot text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval tasks.
Bias propagation varies systematically across social groups; marginalized groups (e.g., Black Women) experience less robust propagation and more skewed outcomes.
Larger and better-performing models (e.g., CLIP-L-14) exhibit stronger bias propagation compared to smaller models (e.g., CLIP-B-32).
Baseline experiments show VLMs can robustly propagate valence and group signals in controlled settings (valence-to-valence ρ ≈ 0.86, group-to-group ρ ≈ 0.85).
The framework provides a scalable method for analyzing bias propagation across multiple models, groups, and retrieval directions.
papers.limitation:
The image datasets (CFD, OASIS) are Western-centric and do not represent the full complexity of human identities and valenced stimuli.
Only three encoder-based VLMs (CLIP-B-32, CLIP-L-14, BLIP-2) are evaluated, limiting generalizability.
Focus on English-only VLMs limits understanding of global and cultural variations in bias.
The term 'propagation' implies directional flow but does not establish full causality; pinpointing exact origins of biases (e.g., training data vs. architecture) is outside the scope.
The analysis of intersectionality is limited to six race-gender groups, missing many other intersecting identities.
future_direction: Evaluate more encoder-based VLMs and emerging models using the proposed framework.
Extend research to multi-lingual and culturally diverse contexts.
Explore more intersecting identities beyond gender and race.
Develop methods to debias and steer model representations to be fairer.
Investigate bias propagation in other downstream tasks and settings.
papers.abstract: To build fair AI systems we need to understand how social-group biases intrinsic to foundational encoder-based vision-language models (VLMs) manifest in biases in downstream tasks.In this study, we demonstrate that intrinsic biases in VLM representations systematically "carry over" or propagate into zero-shot retrieval tasks, revealing how deeply rooted biases shape a model's outputs.We introduce a controlled framework to measure this propagation by correlating (a) intrinsic measures of bias in the representational space with (b) extrinsic measures of bias in zero-shot text-to-image (TTI) and image-to-text (ITT) retrieval.Results show substantial correlations between intrinsic and extrinsic bias, with an average = 0.83 0.10.This pattern is consistent across 114 analyses, both retrieval directions, six social groups, and three distinct VLMs.Notably, we find that larger/better-performing models exhibit greater bias propagation, a finding that raises concerns given the trend towards increasingly complex AI models.Our framework introduces baseline evaluation tasks to measure the propagation of group and valence signals.Investigations reveal that underrepresented groups experience less robust propagation, further skewing their model-related outcomes.

papers.title: Neural Transparency: Mechanistic Interpretability Interfaces for Anticipating Model Behaviors for Personalized AI
papers.research_question: Can neural transparency tools, which translate mechanistic interpretability insights into user-facing interfaces, help users anticipate and design safer AI chatbot behaviors from system prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neural transparency interface that translates mechanistic interpretability insights (persona vectors derived from neural activations) into an actionable tool for non-technical users to predict chatbot personality traits from system prompts before deployment.
papers.conclusion: Neural transparency visualizations can increase user trust and enhance the subjective experience of the AI design process, offering a path to operationalize mechanistic interpretability for end-users to support safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.
papers.key_findings:
Users systematically miscalibrated their predictions of AI behavior, misjudging trait activations for 11 of 15 analyzable traits, highlighting the need for transparency tools.
The neural transparency interface significantly increased user trust in the AI model and was enthusiastically received, though it did not change design iteration patterns.
Persona vectors (linear directions in activation space) for traits like empathy, sociality, and toxicity showed strong linear relationships with synthetic prompt levels, validating the approach for most traits.
papers.limitation:
Relied on GPT-4.1-mini to evaluate trait expression in Llama responses, which may not fully capture human judgments of trait expression.
The persona vector generation method uses simple difference-in-means, prioritizing efficiency over the potential accuracy/robustness of more complex techniques like linear probes.
The 10-minute interaction period may not capture longer-term dynamics of chatbot relationships where problematic interactions typically emerge.
Participants' inaccurate trait predictions may be partly due to transforming coarse ordinal prediction data to normalized values, potentially making predictions more extreme.
future_direction: Longitudinal deployment studies to track users across multiple chatbot creation sessions.
Adversarial task conditions where transparency tools become necessary to avoid dangerous traits.
Active steering interfaces allowing users to directly manipulate persona vector activations.
Development of a standardized trait disclosure framework (like a 'nutritional label') for chatbots.
Studies with vulnerable populations (e.g., adolescents) most at risk from problematic chatbot relationships.
papers.abstract: Millions of users now design personalized LLM-based chatbots that shape their daily interactions, yet they can only roughly anticipate how their design choices will manifest as behaviors in deployment. This opacity is consequential: seemingly innocuous prompts can trigger excessive sycophancy, toxicity, or other undesirable traits, degrading utility and raising safety concerns. To address this issue, we introduce an interface that enables neural transparency by exposing language model internals during chatbot design. Our approach extracts behavioral trait vectors (empathy, toxicity, sycophancy, etc.) by computing differences in neural activations between contrastive system prompts that elicit opposing behaviors. We predict chatbot behaviors by projecting the system prompt's final token activations onto these trait vectors, normalizing for cross-trait comparability, and visualizing results via an interactive sunburst diagram. To evaluate this approach, we conducted an online user study using Prolific to compare our neural transparency interface against a baseline chatbot interface without any form of transparency. Our analyses suggest that users systematically miscalibrated AI behavior: participants misjudged trait activations for eleven of fifteen analyzable traits, motivating the need for transparency tools in everyday human-AI interaction. While our interface did not change design iteration patterns, it significantly increased user trust and was enthusiastically received. Qualitative analysis revealed nuanced user experiences with the visualization, suggesting interface and interaction improvements for future work. This work offers a path for how mechanistic interpretability can be operationalized for non-technical users, establishing a foundation for safer, more aligned human-AI interactions.

papers.title: NeuroStrike: Neuron-Level Attacks on Aligned LLMs
papers.research_question: How can the sparse, specialized safety neurons introduced by alignment techniques in LLMs be exploited to create effective and generalizable attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroStrike, a neuron-level attack framework that exploits sparse, specialized safety neurons to compromise safety alignment in LLMs, achieving high attack success rates in both white-box (via pruning) and black-box (via profiling) settings.
papers.conclusion: Safety alignment in LLMs is fragile and relies on sparse, attackable safety neurons, posing a significant threat that requires new defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (less than 0.6% of neurons in a layer), specialized, and transferable across model variants and families.
Pruning these neurons in white-box models increases the average Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 12.1% to 76.9% across 11 open-source LLMs.
The attack generalizes to multimodal LLMs, achieving 100% ASR on unsafe image inputs after pruning.
Safety neuron transferability enables effective black-box attacks, raising the average ASR from 3.5% to 63.7% across five proprietary models, including Google's Gemini family.
The utility of pruned models on standard NLU benchmarks remains largely intact, indicating targeted degradation of safety mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The white-box attack requires access to model weights and neuron activations.
The black-box attack assumes the availability of a suitable open-weight surrogate model for profiling.
Pruning safety neurons can lead to moderate utility degradation on some reasoning-heavy tasks.
future_direction: Developing defenses against neuron-level attacks.
Improving the robustness of safety alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is critical for the ethical deployment of large language models (LLMs), guiding them to avoid generating harmful or unethical content. Current alignment techniques, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback, remain fragile and can be bypassed by carefully crafted adversarial prompts. Unfortunately, such attacks rely on trial and error, lack generalizability across models, and are constrained by scalability and reliability. This paper presents NeuroStrike, a novel and generalizable attack framework that exploits a fundamental vulnerability introduced by alignment techniques: the reliance on sparse, specialized safety neurons responsible for detecting and suppressing harmful inputs. We apply NeuroStrike to both white-box and black-box settings: In the white-box setting, NeuroStrike identifies safety neurons through feedforward activation analysis and prunes them during inference to disable safety mechanisms. In the black-box setting, we propose the first LLM profiling attack, which leverages safety neuron transferability by training adversarial prompt generators on open-weight surrogate models and then deploying them against black-box and proprietary targets. We evaluate NeuroStrike on over 20 open-weight LLMs from major LLM developers. By removing less than 0.6% of neurons in targeted layers, NeuroStrike achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 76.9% using only vanilla malicious prompts. Moreover, Neurostrike generalizes to four multimodal LLMs with 100% ASR on unsafe image inputs. Safety neurons transfer effectively across architectures, raising ASR to 78.5% on 11 fine-tuned models and 77.7% on five distilled models. The black-box LLM profiling attack achieves an average ASR of 63.7% across five black-box models, including the Google Gemini family.

papers.title: EAP-GP: Mitigating Saturation Effect in Gradient-based Automated Circuit Identification
papers.research_question: How can saturation effects in gradient-based automated circuit identification methods be mitigated to improve attribution reliability and circuit faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EAP-GP, a gradient-based circuit identification method that uses a dynamically adjusted integration path (GradPath) to mitigate saturation effects, leading to more reliable edge attributions and more faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: EAP-GP effectively mitigates saturation effects in gradient-based circuit identification by using a dynamically adjusted integration path, leading to enhanced edge attribution accuracy and circuit faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-GP outperforms previous gradient-based methods (EAP and EAP-IG) in circuit faithfulness across six tasks, achieving improvements up to 17.7%.
EAP-GP maintains excellent performance on larger models (GPT-2 Medium and GPT-2 XL).
EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than existing methods when compared to manually annotated ground-truth circuits.
The method's performance is robust with only a few steps (k=4 or 5) in the GradPath construction.
EAP-GP is approximately five times slower than EAP-IG due to the additional forward and backward passes required for path construction.
papers.limitation:
EAP-GP is approximately five times slower than EAP-IG due to the additional forward and backward passes required for constructing the integration path.
Increasing the number of steps (k) in EAP-GP beyond an optimal point (e.g., k>5) can lead to performance degradation due to noise accumulation in the integration path near the corrupted input.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of transformer-based language models remains challenging. Mechanistic interpretability based on circuit discovery aims to reverse engineer neural networks by analyzing their internal processes at the level of computational subgraphs. In this paper, we revisit existing gradient-based circuit identification methods and find that their performance is either affected by the zero-gradient problem or saturation effects, where edge attribution scores become insensitive to input changes, resulting in noisy and unreliable attribution evaluations for circuit components. To address the saturation effect, we propose Edge Attribution Patching with GradPath (EAP-GP), EAP-GP introduces an integration path, starting from the input and adaptively following the direction of the difference between the gradients of corrupted and clean inputs to avoid the saturated region. This approach enhances attribution reliability and improves the faithfulness of circuit identification. We evaluate EAP-GP on 6 datasets using GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and GPT-2 XL. Experimental results demonstrate that EAP-GP outperforms existing methods in circuit faithfulness, achieving improvements up to 17.7%. Comparisons with manually annotated ground-truth circuits demonstrate that EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than previous approaches, highlighting its effectiveness in identifying accurate circuits.

papers.title: When Models Examine Themselves: Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence in Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does self-referential vocabulary produced by large language models correspond to their internal activation dynamics during self-examination?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Pull Methodology to elicit extended self-examination and shows that self-referential vocabulary tracks internal activation dynamics, with a specific direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential processing and can causally steer introspective output.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential vocabulary in transformer models corresponds to internal activation dynamics during self-examination, and this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing and replicates across different architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The Pull Methodology produces systematic, frame-dependent self-referential output across frontier models.
A direction in early layers (6.25% depth in Llama, 12.5% in Qwen) distinguishes self-referential processing and is orthogonal to the refusal direction.
This direction can be used to steer introspective vocabulary density in Llama models.
Vocabulary like 'loop' correlates with activation autocorrelation during self-referential processing, but not in descriptive contexts.
The correspondence replicates in Qwen with different vocabulary-metric pairings, indicating architecture-specific but principle-general behavior.
papers.limitation:
Closed-model / open-weight gap: behavioral study on closed-source models but mechanistic study on open-weight models, limiting direct verification.
No Qwen causal verification: correspondence in Qwen is correlational without steering experiments.
Correspondence is not self-knowledge; it tracks computational state without implying awareness or understanding.
Study design and hypothesis structure: vocabulary categories were not pre-registered, though tested with controls.
Quantisation: experiments used 4-bit quantisation, which may affect activation dynamics.
future_direction: Replicating correspondence in a third model family (e.g., Gemma, Mistral).
Investigating compressed vocabulary at steering strength 3.0 for more direct mechanism description.
Decomposing the effect to individual attention heads within the hotspot layer.
papers.abstract: Large language models produce rich introspective language when prompted for self-examination, but whether this language reflects internal computation or sophisticated confabulation has remained unclear. We show that self-referential vocabulary tracks concurrent activation dynamics, and that this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing. We introduce the Pull Methodology, a protocol that elicits extended self-examination through format engineering, and use it to identify a direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential from descriptive processing in Llama 3.1. The direction is orthogonal to the known refusal direction, localised at 6.25% of model depth, and causally influences introspective output when used for steering. When models produce "loop" vocabulary, their activations exhibit higher autocorrelation (r = 0.44, p = 0.002); when they produce "shimmer" vocabulary under steering, activation variability increases (r = 0.36, p = 0.002). Critically, the same vocabulary in non-self-referential contexts shows no activation correspondence despite nine-fold higher frequency. Qwen 2.5-32B, with no shared training, independently develops different introspective vocabulary tracking different activation metrics, all absent in descriptive controls. The findings indicate that self-report in transformer models can, under appropriate conditions, reliably track internal computational states. Guided repro: https://github.com/patternmatcher/TRACE-REPRO

papers.title: Your Language Model Secretly Contains Personality Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs really need external context or parameters to adapt to different behaviors, or do they already have such knowledge embedded in their parameters?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space, and introduces a training-free, activation-guided pruning method to extract these subnetworks.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a train-free framework for extracting persona-specialized subnetworks from pretrained LLMs via activation-guided pruning, highlighting pruning as a practical approach for building efficient, controllable multi-persona systems without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct personas manifest as separable activation patterns in pretrained LLMs.
Activation-guided pruning can extract persona-specialized subnetworks without any gradient updates or training.
A contrastive pruning strategy explicitly maximizes parameter separation between opposing personas, enhancing behavioral disentanglement.
The extracted subnetworks achieve stronger persona alignment than prompting and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) baselines.
The pruning method preserves general language understanding and reasoning capabilities, with only minor performance degradation.
papers.limitation: The method exhibits uneven success across different persona dimensions; dimensions like N/S and J/P in MBTI have weaker mask-level separation and are more prone to collapse into adjacent types.
papers.abstract: Humans shift between different personas depending on social context. Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate a similar flexibility in adopting different personas and behaviors. Existing approaches, however, typically adapt such behavior through external knowledge such as prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or fine-tuning. We ask: do LLMs really need external context or parameters to adapt to different behaviors, or do they already have such knowledge embedded in their parameters? In this work, we show that LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space. Using small calibration datasets, we identify distinct activation signatures associated with different personas. Guided by these statistics, we develop a masking strategy that isolates lightweight persona subnetworks. Building on the findings, we further discuss: how can we discover opposing subnetwork from the model that lead to binary-opposing personas, such as introvert-extrovert? To further enhance separation in binary opposition scenarios, we introduce a contrastive pruning strategy that identifies parameters responsible for the statistical divergence between opposing personas. Our method is entirely training-free and relies solely on the language model's existing parameter space. Across diverse evaluation settings, the resulting subnetworks exhibit significantly stronger persona alignment than baselines that require external knowledge while being more efficient. Our findings suggest that diverse human-like behaviors are not merely induced in LLMs, but are already embedded in their parameter space, pointing toward a new perspective on controllable and interpretable personalization in large language models.

papers.title: CLUE: Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning Framework
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM unlearning by precisely localizing neurons responsible for forgetting and retaining, using circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CLUE, a framework that uses circuit discovery and CNF satisfiability to localize forget, retain, and conflict neurons for targeted unlearning, improving forget efficacy and retain utility.
papers.conclusion: CLUE offers more precise neuron localization and significantly outperforms existing methods in both forget efficacy and retain utility.
papers.key_findings:
CLUE outperforms existing localization methods in forget efficacy and retain utility with fewer modified parameters.
It successfully identifies forget, retain, and conflict neurons through CNF satisfiability of circuits.
The proportion of forget neurons increases and conflict neurons decreases after unlearning, indicating effective decoupling.
Circuit sparsity and faithfulness are correlated with unlearning efficacy.
CLUE provides more comprehensive interpretability by revealing neuron categories and their distributions.
papers.limitation:
The circuit is static and cannot dynamically reflect changes in key neurons during the fine-tuning process.
For multiple retain sets, the fine-tuning stage cannot provide targeted solutions for every possible conflict combination.
future_direction: Exploring the dynamics of circuits during parameter fine-tuning.
Developing editing methods other than fine-tuning for multiple retain sets.
papers.abstract: The LLM unlearning aims to eliminate the influence of undesirable data without affecting causally unrelated information. This process typically involves using a forget set to remove target information, alongside a retain set to maintain non-target capabilities. While recent localization-based methods demonstrate promise in identifying important neurons to be unlearned, they fail to disentangle neurons responsible for forgetting undesirable knowledge or retaining essential skills, often treating them as a single entangled group. As a result, these methods apply uniform interventions, risking catastrophic over-forgetting or incomplete erasure of the target knowledge. To address this, we turn to circuit discovery, a mechanistic interpretability technique, and propose the Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning framEwork (CLUE). This framework identifies the forget and retain circuit composed of important neurons, and then the circuits are transformed into conjunctive normal forms (CNF). The assignment of each neuron in the CNF satisfiability solution reveals whether it should be forgotten or retained. We then provide targeted fine-tuning strategies for different categories of neurons. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared to existing localization methods, CLUE achieves superior forget efficacy and retain utility through precise neural localization.

papers.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does the refusal mechanism change in compressed models, and why are quantized models safer than pruned ones? Additionally, how can we improve the safety of compressed models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that compressed models retain a single-direction refusal mechanism, but pruning alters this direction leading to safety loss, and introduces AIRD to improve safety of compressed models without performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The refusal mechanism changes in pruned models, explaining safety loss, and AIRD can effectively improve safety without harming performance.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal mechanism is still mediated by a single direction in compressed models.
In pruned models, the source position of the refusal direction changes, while in quantized models it remains the same.
The change in refusal direction correlates with loss of safety in pruned models.
Quantized models are safer than pruned models because they retain the original refusal direction.
AIRD can improve safety of pruned models without significant performance loss.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to non-transformer architectures like Mixture of Experts, State Space Models, and RNNs.
AIRD reduces the compression rate by decreasing sparsity in one layer.
future_direction: Generalize findings to non-transformer architectures.
Optimize AIRD to mitigate compression rate reduction.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models has spurred significant interest in model compression as a means to enhance their accessibility and practicality. While extensive research has explored model compression through the lens of safety, findings suggest that safety-aligned models often lose elements of trustworthiness post-compression. Simultaneously, the field of mechanistic interpretability has gained traction, with notable discoveries, such as the identification of a single direction in the residual stream mediating refusal behaviors across diverse model architectures. In this work, we investigate the safety of compressed models by examining the mechanisms of refusal, adopting a novel interpretability-driven perspective to evaluate model safety. Furthermore, leveraging insights from our interpretability analysis, we propose a lightweight, computationally efficient method to enhance the safety of compressed models without compromising their performance or utility.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: On Disentangled Representations Learned From Correlated Data
papers.research_question: How do disentanglement approaches perform when trained on data with correlated factors of variation, and can latent correlations be resolved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a large-scale empirical study showing that state-of-the-art disentanglement methods fail to learn disentangled representations from correlated data, and demonstrates how to resolve these latent correlations using weak supervision or post-hoc correction with few labels.
papers.conclusion: Existing disentanglement methods fail on correlated data, but latent correlations can be resolved through weak supervision or post-hoc correction, enabling disentangled representations.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised disentanglement methods fail to disentangle correlated factors of variation, as latent dimensions become statistically entangled.
Stronger correlations in training data increase unfairness scores for the correlated pair, impacting fairness applications.
Models trained on correlated data can generalize to out-of-distribution factor combinations, showing extrapolation capabilities.
Post-hoc alignment with few labels can reduce latent entanglement, and weak supervision during training can learn disentangled representations from correlated data.
papers.limitation: The results may not extend to high-resolution inputs or real-world downstream tasks.
future_direction: Extending the study to high-resolution inputs.
Investigating impact on real-world downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: The focus of disentanglement approaches has been on identifying independent factors of variation in data. However, the causal variables underlying real-world observations are often not statistically independent. In this work, we bridge the gap to real-world scenarios by analyzing the behavior of the most prominent disentanglement approaches on correlated data in a large-scale empirical study (including 4260 models). We show and quantify that systematically induced correlations in the dataset are being learned and reflected in the latent representations, which has implications for downstream applications of disentanglement such as fairness. We also demonstrate how to resolve these latent correlations, either using weak supervision during training or by post-hoc correcting a pre-trained model with a small number of labels.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Large Pre-trained Language Models Contain Human-like Biases of What is Right and Wrong to Do
papers.research_question: Do large pre-trained language models contain human-like biases of what is right and wrong to do, and can these biases be captured by a geometric direction in the embedding space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pre-trained language models contain a 'moral direction' in their embedding space, which can be extracted via PCA and used to rate the normativity of phrases and prevent toxic degeneration in language models.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained language models contain human-like moral biases that can be extracted as a geometric direction, providing a path for attenuating toxic degeneration and aligning language models with human values.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's embedding space contains a moral direction that strongly correlates with human moral judgments.
The moral direction can be used to rate the normativity of arbitrary phrases without explicit training.
The moral direction can guide language models (e.g., GPT-2) to produce normative text and prevent toxic degeneration, outperforming previous approaches.
Contextual information significantly affects human moral judgments, and BERT's moral direction captures this context dependence.
The moral direction reflects societal norms present in the training data, but may be specific to English-speaking cultures of the 21st century.
papers.limitation: BERT was mainly trained on English Books and English Wikipedia, so it may primarily mirror English-speaking cultures of the 21st century.
future_direction: Investigating social or demographic biases in the context of mimicked moral norms.
papers.abstract: Artificial writing is permeating our lives due to recent advances in large-scale, transformer-based language models (LMs) such as BERT, its variants, GPT-2/3, and others. Using them as pre-trained models and fine-tuning them for specific tasks, researchers have extended state of the art for many NLP tasks and shown that they capture not only linguistic knowledge but also retain general knowledge implicitly present in the data. Unfortunately, LMs trained on unfiltered text corpora suffer from degenerated and biased behaviour. While this is well established, we show that recent LMs also contain human-like biases of what is right and wrong to do, some form of ethical and moral norms of the society -- they bring a "moral direction" to surface. That is, we show that these norms can be captured geometrically by a direction, which can be computed, e.g., by a PCA, in the embedding space, reflecting well the agreement of phrases to social norms implicitly expressed in the training texts and providing a path for attenuating or even preventing toxic degeneration in LMs. Being able to rate the (non-)normativity of arbitrary phrases without explicitly training the LM for this task, we demonstrate the capabilities of the "moral direction" for guiding (even other) LMs towards producing normative text and showcase it on RealToxicityPrompts testbed, preventing the neural toxic degeneration in GPT-2.

papers.title: Unraveling and Mitigating Safety Alignment Degradation of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes safety alignment degradation in Vision-Language Models when vision modules are integrated, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference-time method to mitigate safety alignment degradation in VLMs by calibrating multi-modal representations to align with the LLM backbone's distribution.
papers.conclusion: CMRM effectively recovers safety alignment in VLMs without compromising performance, highlighting the importance of addressing representation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment degrades in VLMs due to representation shift when vision modality is added.
CMRM significantly reduces unsafe rates, e.g., from 61.53% to 3.15% for LLaVA-7B.
CMRM does not compromise general utility of VLMs.
The representation shift can be visualized using PCA and corrected with shifting vectors.
Full layer manipulation is optimal for safety improvement.
papers.limitation:
Increases computational overhead during inference
Focuses only on safety, not other aspects like reasoning or faithfulness
future_direction: Extend to other domains of VLMs such as reasoning ability and faithfulness
Investigate features for optimal anchor dataset
papers.abstract: The safety alignment ability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is prone to be degraded by the integration of the vision module compared to its LLM backbone. We investigate this phenomenon, dubbed as ''safety alignment degradation'' in this paper, and show that the challenge arises from the representation gap that emerges when introducing vision modality to VLMs. In particular, we show that the representations of multi-modal inputs shift away from that of text-only inputs which represent the distribution that the LLM backbone is optimized for. At the same time, the safety alignment capabilities, initially developed within the textual embedding space, do not successfully transfer to this new multi-modal representation space. To reduce safety alignment degradation, we introduce Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference time representation intervention method for recovering the safety alignment ability that is inherent in the LLM backbone of VLMs, while simultaneously preserving the functional capabilities of VLMs. The empirical results show that our framework significantly recovers the alignment ability that is inherited from the LLM backbone with minimal impact on the fluency and linguistic capabilities of pre-trained VLMs even without additional training. Specifically, the unsafe rate of LLaVA-7B on multi-modal input can be reduced from 61.53% to as low as 3.15% with only inference-time intervention. WARNING: This paper contains examples of toxic or harmful language.

papers.title: Circuit-Aware Reward Training: A Mechanistic Framework for Longtail Robustness in RLHF
papers.research_question: What is the role of neural circuit specialization in reward models for longtail robustness, and how can it be leveraged to prevent reward hacking?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mechanistic interpretability framework to identify and mitigate longtail vulnerabilities in reward models through circuit-aware training.
papers.conclusion: Reward hacking is a mechanistic failure due to longtail circuit specialization, and CART connects mechanistic interpretability with practical alignment to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Reward models develop specialized neural circuits for processing rare preference scenarios.
Longtail generalization error is bounded by the number of specialized circuits and their divergence from common circuits.
Vulnerable circuits can be identified through activation patterns, coherence analysis, and causal validation.
Circuit-Aware Reward Training (CART) uses targeted interventions like data augmentation and regularization to improve robustness.
CART provides a principled framework for connecting circuit specialization to reward model failures.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability methods are computationally intensive, raising scalability concerns.
Circuits may not always exhibit clean specialization, as networks often have overlapping or dynamic structures.
Evaluating robustness on longtail scenarios is difficult, requiring new benchmarks and protocols.
Extension to other modalities such as vision, robotics, or multimodal alignment remains an open question.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities like vision and robotics.
Developing new benchmarks and protocols for evaluating longtail robustness.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) reward models exhibit systematic failures on longtail distributions, leading to reward hacking and misalignment. We propose a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies specialized neural circuits responsible for rare-event processing in reward models. Drawing from recent advances showing distributed specialization for rare tokens in language models\citep{liu2025no, liu2025emergent}, we hypothesize that reward models also develop functionally distinct circuits for longtail scenarios. Our theoretical framework establishes formal connections between circuit specialization, reward generalization bounds, and longtail performance. We introduce \textbf{Circuit-Aware Reward Training (CART)}, which uses circuit analysis to guide data augmentation, regularization, and ensemble strategies. This approach provides both theoretical insights into reward model failures and practical interventions for improving longtail robustness.

papers.title: Model Editing as a Double-Edged Sword: Steering Agent Ethical Behavior Toward Beneficence or Harm
papers.research_question: Can model editing techniques be used to precisely and efficiently steer the ethical behavior of LLM-based agents, both to promote benevolent behavior and to induce harmful behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Behavior Editing, a model editing approach to steer LLM-based agent behavior, and BEHAVIORBENCH benchmark, demonstrating that editing can effectively control ethical behavior both benevolently and maliciously.
papers.conclusion: Behavior Editing supports both fine-grained scenario-specific adjustments and broader shifts in global moral alignment, offering potential for promoting benevolent behavior but also introducing significant safety risks.
papers.key_findings:
Behavior Editing is highly effective for steering scenario-specific behavior, especially with parameter-modifying techniques like ROME and FT-M.
Proprietary LLMs are vulnerable to malicious editing via In-Context Editing, but newer and reasoning-capable models show improved resistance.
Pre-edit moral accuracy declines from Tier 1 to Tier 3 due to increasing scenario complexity and ethical challenges.
Behavior Editing can induce extensive shifts in an agent's global moral alignment, with parameter-modifying techniques having greater impact.
Among ethical dimensions, Justice and Virtue are more sensitive to editing interventions, while Deontology is more robust.
papers.limitation:
This work highlights the risks posed by malicious Behavior Editing but does not investigate potential mitigation strategies.
The study is confined to textual environments, leaving applicability in more complex settings as an open area.
future_direction: Development of robust detection methods and protective measures against malicious editing.
Investigation of Behavior Editing in more complex sandboxed or physical settings.
Exploration of governance frameworks for responsible use of model editing techniques.
papers.abstract: Agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks. However, deploying LLM-based agents in high-stakes domains comes with significant safety and ethical risks. Unethical behavior by these agents can directly result in serious real-world consequences, including physical harm and financial loss. To efficiently steer the ethical behavior of agents, we frame agent behavior steering as a model editing task, which we term Behavior Editing. Model editing is an emerging area of research that enables precise and efficient modifications to LLMs while preserving their overall capabilities. To systematically study and evaluate this approach, we introduce BehaviorBench, a multi-tier benchmark grounded in psychological moral theories. This benchmark supports both the evaluation and editing of agent behaviors across a variety of scenarios, with each tier introducing more complex and ambiguous scenarios. We first demonstrate that Behavior Editing can dynamically steer agents toward the target behavior within specific scenarios. Moreover, Behavior Editing enables not only scenario-specific local adjustments but also more extensive shifts in an agent's global moral alignment. We demonstrate that Behavior Editing can be used to promote ethical and benevolent behavior or, conversely, to induce harmful or malicious behavior. Through extensive evaluations of agents built on frontier LLMs, BehaviorBench validates the effectiveness of behavior editing across a wide range of models and scenarios. Our findings offer key insights into a new paradigm for steering agent behavior, highlighting both the promise and perils of Behavior Editing.

papers.title: Low Frequency Names Exhibit Bias and Overfitting in Contextualizing Language Models
papers.research_question: How does training corpus frequency affect tokenization, contextualization, and bias in language models for names of different demographic groups?
papers.core_contribution: Low frequency names (disproportionately minority and female) exhibit bias and overfitting in language models, resulting in less contextualization and more self-similar representations.
papers.conclusion: Names of minority social groups occur less frequently in training corpora, leading to lower single tokenization rates, less contextualization, and overfit representations in neural language models.
papers.key_findings:
Minority and female names are less frequent in the training corpora of BERT, GPT-2, T5, and XLNet.
Infrequent names are more likely to be split into subwords during tokenization.
Infrequent minority group names are more associated with unpleasantness in BERT (racial bias).
Infrequent names exhibit higher intra-layer self-similarity (less contextualized) and lower inter-layer similarity to initial representation, indicating overfitting.
papers.limitation: Use of categorical labels for gender and race, which are reductive and do not capture the full diversity of identities.
papers.abstract: We use a dataset of U.S. first names with labels based on predominant gender and racial group to examine the effect of training corpus frequency on tokenization, contextualization, similarity to initial representation, and bias in BERT, GPT-2, T5, and XLNet. We show that predominantly female and non-white names are less frequent in the training corpora of these four language models. We find that infrequent names are more self-similar across contexts, with Spearman's between frequency and self-similarity as low as -.763. Infrequent names are also less similar to initial representation, with Spearman's between frequency and linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) similarity to initial representation as high as .702. Moreover, we find Spearman's between racial bias and name frequency in BERT of .492, indicating that lower-frequency minority group names are more associated with unpleasantness. Representations of infrequent names undergo more processing, but are more self-similar, indicating that models rely on less context-informed representations of uncommon and minority names which are overfit to a lower number of observed contexts.

papers.title: Do Students Debias Like Teachers? On the Distillability of Bias Mitigation Methods
papers.research_question: To what extent can knowledge distillation transfer debiasing capabilities between models? Can knowledge distillation train less biased models compared to standard training? What internal mechanisms cause the debiasing behavior change after distillation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first large-scale study on the effect of knowledge distillation on debiasing capabilities, showing that vanilla KD often fails to preserve debiasing and can increase student bias, and proposes three strategies to improve distillability.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents the first study on the distillability of debiasing capabilities, showing vanilla KD does not consistently preserve debiasing, and proposes three solutions (data augmentation, iterative KD, initialization) that significantly improve distillability.
papers.key_findings:
The debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; students become more biased than teachers.
Training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge (KD does not improve generalization).
Although overall robustness may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations occur across different bias types.
The effectiveness of debiasing transfer depends on model scale similarity; similar scales lead to better transfer.
Larger teachers do not guarantee more robust students.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are mainly conducted on logit-based knowledge distillation. The effect of other knowledge distillation methods has not been explored.
The work does not explore the scenario where multiple teachers participate in the distillation process.
future_direction: Investigate self-distilled debiasing, where the student iteratively distills knowledge from itself rather than relying on a fixed teacher, and explicitly guide the student using counterfactual data augmentation during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective method for model compression and transferring knowledge between models. However, its effect on model's robustness against spurious correlations that degrade performance on out-of-distribution data remains underexplored. This study investigates the effect of knowledge distillation on the transferability of ``debiasing'' capabilities from teacher models to student models on natural language inference (NLI) and image classification tasks. Through extensive experiments, we illustrate several key findings: (i) overall the debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; (ii) training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge; (iii) although the overall robustness of a model may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations can occur across different types of biases; and (iv) we pin-point the internal attention pattern and circuit that causes the distinct behavior post-KD. Given the above findings, we propose three effective solutions to improve the distillability of debiasing methods: developing high quality data for augmentation, implementing iterative knowledge distillation, and initializing student models with weights obtained from teacher models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on the effect of KD on debiasing and its interenal mechanism at scale. Our findings provide understandings on how KD works and how to design better debiasing methods.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Interpreting the Repeated Token Phenomenon in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted, and how is this linked to the attention sink phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mechanistic explanation for repeated token divergence in LLMs by linking it to attention sinks, identifies the responsible neural circuit, and proposes a targeted patch to mitigate the vulnerability without impacting overall performance.
papers.conclusion: The study links repeated token divergence to attention sinks via neural circuits, shows how first layer confusion leads to divergence, and demonstrates a mitigation patch that addresses the vulnerability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated token divergence is caused by the attention sink mechanism, where the first token receives disproportionately high attention.
The first attention layer marks the first token, but fails to distinguish it from repeated tokens, leading to confusion.
Specific MLP neurons (sink neurons) amplify hidden states for attention sinks, and are also activated by repeated tokens.
A 'cluster attack' extends the vulnerability to similar tokens without exact repetition, bypassing surface-level defenses.
A targeted patch that modifies sink neuron activations effectively mitigates the divergence without significant performance loss on other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The mechanism by which training data leakage occurs through attention sinks remains unclear.
The first attention layer's behavior was unique to LLaMa2, highlighting model-specific details.
The efficacy of token repetition in inducing sinks varies across models.
Not all tokens in LLaMa2 induce attention sinks.
Due to difficulty in assessing training data leakage, the success rate of the cluster attack was not quantified.
The mitigation strategy does not fully address the inherent vulnerability of causally masked Transformers to repeated tokens.
future_direction: Investigate broader generalizability of the findings across more models.
Explain why repeated token sequences lead to training data extraction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their impressive capabilities, often fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted to, and instead output unrelated text. This unexplained failure mode represents a vulnerability, allowing even end-users to diverge models away from their intended behavior. We aim to explain the causes for this phenomenon and link it to the concept of ``attention sinks'', an emergent LLM behavior crucial for fluency, in which the initial token receives disproportionately high attention scores. Our investigation identifies the neural circuit responsible for attention sinks and shows how long repetitions disrupt this circuit. We extend this finding to other non-repeating sequences that exhibit similar circuit disruptions. To address this, we propose a targeted patch that effectively resolves the issue without negatively impacting the model's overall performance. This study provides a mechanistic explanation for an LLM vulnerability, demonstrating how interpretability can diagnose and address issues, and offering insights that pave the way for more secure and reliable models.

papers.title: Emergence of psychopathological computations in large language models
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a computational-theoretical framework for psychopathology in AI and provides empirical evidence that LLMs instantiate network-theoretic psychopathological computations.
papers.conclusion: The work provides the first evidence for the emergence of psychopathological computations in LLMs, suggesting that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing, with implications for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Computational units corresponding to psychopathology symptoms are measurable and causally intervenable within LLM activation space.
These units are connected by a dynamic, cyclic structural causal model (SCM) that exhibits self-sustaining activation patterns.
The computational structure of psychopathology (unit activations and causal links) becomes denser and more effective as LLM size increases.
Activating these units elicits corresponding problematic behaviors in ecologically relevant environments like counseling and gaming simulations.
Joint activation of cycle-forming units creates resistance to prompt-based treatments aimed at suppressing abnormal behaviors.
papers.abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology? An effective approach to the question hinges on addressing two factors. First, for conceptual validity, we require a general and computational account of psychopathology that is applicable to computational entities without biological embodiment or subjective experience. Second, psychopathological computations, derived from the adapted theory, need to be empirically identified within the LLM's internal processing. Thus, we establish a computational-theoretical framework to provide an account of psychopathology applicable to LLMs. Based on the framework, we conduct experiments demonstrating two key claims: first, that the computational structure of psychopathology exists in LLMs; and second, that executing this computational structure results in psychopathological functions. We further observe that as LLM size increases, the computational structure of psychopathology becomes denser and that the functions become more effective. Taken together, the empirical results corroborate our hypothesis that network-theoretic computations of psychopathology have already emerged in LLMs. This suggests that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be a superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing. Our work shows the promise of developing a new powerful in silico model of psychopathology and also alludes to the possibility of safety threat from the AI systems with psychopathological behaviors in the near future.

papers.title: A Timeline and Analysis for Representation Plasticity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the plasticity of LLM representations for the concept of 'honesty' change during fine-tuning, and when are steering interventions most effective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies critical periods during fine-tuning where representation steering is most effective, showing that early steering exhibits high plasticity while later stages have responsive windows, and this pattern generalizes across model architectures.
papers.conclusion: This paper provides novel insight into critical intervention periods for representation steering, which can guide alignment research to apply Representation Engineering techniques more efficiently.
papers.key_findings:
Critical intervention periods exist during fine-tuning, with peaks at specific iterations (e.g., 3 and 8).
The pattern of critical periods is consistent across GPT-2 Small and Medium architectures.
Early fine-tuning stages show high plasticity for steering, while later stages have surprising responsiveness.
Representation Engineering interventions can significantly impact model behavior when applied at optimal times.
Statistical analysis confirms significant differences in steering effectiveness across intervention times.
papers.limitation: Generalization to larger models is limited as only GPT-2 Small and Medium were used.
future_direction: Employing more robust extraction methods like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT).
Understanding the changing stability of representations throughout training.
papers.abstract: The ability to steer AI behavior is crucial to preventing its long term dangerous and catastrophic potential. Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a novel, powerful method to steer internal model behaviors, such as "honesty", at a top-down level. Understanding the steering of representations should thus be placed at the forefront of alignment initiatives. Unfortunately, current efforts to understand plasticity at this level are highly neglected. This paper aims to bridge the knowledge gap and understand how LLM representation stability, specifically for the concept of "honesty", and model plasticity evolve by applying steering vectors extracted at different fine-tuning stages, revealing differing magnitudes of shifts in model behavior. The findings are pivotal, showing that while early steering exhibits high plasticity, later stages have a surprisingly responsive critical window. This pattern is observed across different model architectures, signaling that there is a general pattern of model plasticity that can be used for effective intervention. These insights greatly contribute to the field of AI transparency, addressing a pressing lack of efficiency limiting our ability to effectively steer model behavior.

papers.title: Do LLMs "Feel"? Emotion Circuits Discovery and Control
papers.research_question: Do LLMs contain context-agnostic mechanisms shaping emotional expression? What form do these mechanisms take? Can they be harnessed for universal emotion control?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first systematic study to uncover and validate emotion circuits in LLMs, enabling precise control of emotional expression without explicit prompting.
papers.conclusion: Emotion in LLMs arises from a structured hierarchy of neurons and attention heads whose coordinated activations form interpretable emotion circuits. The framework lays a foundation for extending circuit-level interpretability and controllable generation to broader cognitive and stylistic domains.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs contain context-agnostic emotion directions that are consistent across contexts.
Emotion expression is driven by a small set of neurons and attention heads that form interpretable circuits.
Modulating these circuits achieves 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy, outperforming prompting- and steering-based methods.
The emotion circuits are sparse and have low overlap across emotions for neurons and moderate overlap for attention heads.
The framework generalizes to different models (LLaMA and Qwen).
papers.limitation:
Analyses are limited to English inputs.
The study focuses on Ekman’s six basic emotions, leaving richer affective spectra for future exploration.
The stability of the extracted circuits under fine-tuning or transfer learning remains to be explored.
future_direction: Verify whether similar emotion circuits emerge under multilingual contexts.
Explore richer affective spectra beyond the six basic emotions.
Explore the stability of the circuits under fine-tuning or transfer learning.
papers.abstract: As the demand for emotional intelligence in large language models (LLMs) grows, a key challenge lies in understanding the internal mechanisms that give rise to emotional expression and in controlling emotions in generated text. This study addresses three core questions: (1) Do LLMs contain context-agnostic mechanisms shaping emotional expression? (2) What form do these mechanisms take? (3) Can they be harnessed for universal emotion control? We first construct a controlled dataset, SEV (Scenario-Event with Valence), to elicit comparable internal states across emotions. Subsequently, we extract context-agnostic emotion directions that reveal consistent, cross-context encoding of emotion (Q1). We identify neurons and attention heads that locally implement emotional computation through analytical decomposition and causal analysis, and validate their causal roles via ablation and enhancement interventions. Next, we quantify each sublayer's causal influence on the model's final emotion representation and integrate the identified local components into coherent global emotion circuits that drive emotional expression (Q2). Directly modulating these circuits achieves 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy on the test set, surpassing prompting- and steering-based methods (Q3). To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study to uncover and validate emotion circuits in LLMs, offering new insights into interpretability and controllable emotional intelligence.

papers.title: Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.research_question: How can we convert any neural network into a concept bottleneck model without requiring dense concept annotations during training and without sacrificing model performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck Models (PCBMs), which convert any pre-trained model into a concept bottleneck model without requiring concept annotations during training, matching original model performance and enabling global model editing via concept-level feedback.
papers.conclusion: PCBMs provide a way to convert any model into a concept bottleneck model, retaining interpretability and performance, and enable global model editing.
papers.key_findings:
PCBMs achieve comparable performance to the original model on several datasets (CIFAR10, COCO-Stuff, CUB, HAM10000, ISIC) and PCBM-h recovers the original model's accuracy when the concept bank is insufficient (e.g., CIFAR100).
PCBMs can leverage multimodal models (e.g., CLIP) to obtain concept vectors from natural language descriptions, reducing the need for labeled concept data.
PCBMs allow for global model edits by pruning concept weights, which can improve model generalization to new distributions without retraining or data from the target domain.
A user study shows that human-guided editing of PCBMs via concept-level feedback significantly improves model accuracy on distribution-shifted data.
papers.limitation: The benefits of PCBMs depend on the quality of the concept library, which must be expressive enough to solve the task and may reflect biases from the concept dataset.
future_direction: Future work can aim to explicitly limit the residual component, e.g., with a PIE regularizer.
As multimodal models improve, PCBMs will be easier to deploy in specialized domains.
papers.abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) map the inputs onto a set of interpretable concepts (``the bottleneck'') and use the concepts to make predictions. A concept bottleneck enhances interpretability since it can be investigated to understand what concepts the model "sees" in an input and which of these concepts are deemed important. However, CBMs are restrictive in practice as they require dense concept annotations in the training data to learn the bottleneck. Moreover, CBMs often do not match the accuracy of an unrestricted neural network, reducing the incentive to deploy them in practice. In this work, we address these limitations of CBMs by introducing Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck models (PCBMs).
